Data Processing. Each UAV was equipped with avionics that recorded for each flight myriad GPS position, ground and air speed, flight trajectory, and other flight metrics many times per second with high spatial accuracy. These data were automatically transmitted during the flights to the control laptop and could be

extracted directly from the avionics units post-flight. The resulting output from each individual flight was a continuous stream of nonparsed data, which we translated to a usable format using a customized dataextraction program (Fernie 2012). The overall translation, extraction, and formatting process followed the detailed procedures and protocols described in H. T. Harvey & Associates (2018). Once the avionics data were extracted and formatted, we matched these data with verified DTBird UAV detection and deterrenttriggering event records based on common timestamps with 1-sec resolution. We then extracted all individually matched flight transects and event records, and combined data from the two study sites to compose the dataset we used to model the response-distance performance characteristics of the DTBird detection and deterrent-triggering functions.

Using the flight-trial data to quantify the probability of DTBird detecting an eagle-surrogate UAV required further processing of the continuous tracking data from each multi-transect flight mission into distinct, independent sample transects. In brief, this involved using ArcGIS 3D Analyst to clip out all tracking data related to loiter-point activity and segment the remaining data into individual, independent flight paths/transects suited to evaluating the probability of detection. Specifically, GIS analysts used 3D Analyst to develop dome-shaped clipping masks and exclude all tracking data beyond 340 m LoS distance from the focal turbine center point at 4–5 m above ground level (i.e., the approximate position of the DTBird cameras on the turbine tower). This clipping distance encompassed the farthest DTBird detections but excluded all loiter tracking, which then allowed for isolating individual sampling flights.

Probability of Detection. To generate estimates of the probability of detecting an eagle-like UAV, we classified each independent flight transect as detected or not detected by the relevant DTBird system, and then calculated the proportions of flight transects in each category at each sampled turbine. The grand-average of the proportions detected at each turbine then represented overall site-specific estimates of the probability of detecting an eagle-like UAV that passed within the expected 240-m maximum detection range of the calibrated DTBird systems.

To generate additional insight about patterns of variability in the probability of detection, we conducted a logistic regression analysis using Systat 13.2.01 (Systat Software, Inc., San Jose, CA). Detected or not detected was the binary response variable, which we evaluated in relation to Site as a categorical predictor, Hour of the Day, and three UAV position metrics: average

Detection Angle, minimum LoS Distance, and average Exposure Direction. (See Supplemental Material S1 for detailed descriptions of the analyzed variables and the full model structure.) To select a final model, we evaluated representative candidate models based on Akaike’s Information Criterion (AIC) scores, log-likelihood ratio chi-square tests, individual parameter tests, and Nagelkerke pseudo-R[2] values (Nagelkerke 1991) to identify a final model given the predictors considered, and to evaluate the relative influences of various predictors on the probability of detection.

Analyzing DTBird’s Response Performance. We developed generalized linear mixed-effect models (GLMMs) to assess the influences of various factors on DTBird’s detection and deterrent-triggering performance. The GLMM statistical framework was particularly suited to analyzing this dataset, because it involved various dependencies and sources of variability. The primary response variable was the LoS distance from the closest DTBird camera at which the UAV was detected or a deterrent event was triggered. This is a metric of fundamental importance because it reflects how early the system identified a potential collision threat and, where relevant, triggered a deterrent signal. The operative assumption was that greater response distances could be interpreted as reflecting an improved detection or triggering response, in that earlier (more distant) detection and targeting was expected to provide more time for the deterrents to alter a target bird’s behavior before the risk of collision became acute. Using 3D Analyst measuring tools, we calculated LoS distances based on the UAV GPS coordinates at the time of each relevant DTBird event. Flight transects included in these analyses were necessarily limited to those that triggered a relevant DTBird response. To fit the response-distance data, we constructed GLMMs to evaluate the influence of various potential random- and fixed-effect predictors hypothesized to influence the response distances. We implemented the models using the lme4 package in R (R Core Team 2023; function lmer, Bates et al. 2015), with a Gaussian distribution and an identity link function.

The final multi-site analysis presented here benefited from insights gained from initial site-specific analyses conducted for the two study sites (e.g., see H. T. Harvey & Associates 2018). Our initial GLMMs included several fixed effects, including environmental variables (sky condition, cloud cover, and light conditions), UAV flight metrics (speed, altitude, and orientation), and DTBird system configurations (camera settings and operational parameters). To account for inherent variations in our experimental setup, we also incorporated random effects for

turbine location and UAV model nested within sites. (See Supplemental Material S2 for detailed descriptions of the full suite of variables considered as the full model for this analysis.) After fitting the full model, we used diagnostic tests to determine if the model violated any GLMM assumptions (Zuur et al. 2009, Wood 2017) using the R package DHARMa (Hartig 2021). Along with residual diagnostics, we evaluated potential combinations of predictors for indications of collinearity, and specifically avoided variable combinations that produced variance inflation factors (VIFs) greater than 5 (Hair et al. 1998, Zuur et al. 2010).

We identified the subset of predictors that best explained variation in the observed response distances via stepwise model selection using the step function in R’s base stats package and following the GLMM model selection guidance of Zuur et al. (2009). This stepwise-selection was done in combination with ANOVA-based and likelihood-ratio test comparisons of nested candidate models and evaluation of AIC scores, Nakagawa pseudo-R[2] values (Nakagawa et al. 2017), and residual plots to select the best model. In considering candidate models, we evaluated only models that met the assumptions of GLMMs. Given the considerable number of predictors and unbalanced categorical factors with some groups having relatively small sample sizes, we used AIC corrected for small sample sizes (AICc) to compare candidate models and avoid overfitting. We generated graphics resulting from the best model using siPlot (Ludecke€ 2023) and emmeans (Length 2023), both of which rely on ggplot2 (Wickham 2016). In discussing the significance of statistical results, we label results with P  0.01 as highly significant, 0.01 , P  0.05 as significant, and 0.05 , P  0.10 as marginally significant.

## RESULTS

Sampling Results. We conducted UAV flight trials at all seven Manzana DTBird installations, with sessions occurring from January through August in 2017 (most concentrated in August), at three Goodnoe Hills DTBird turbines in August 2021, and at four Goodnoe Hills turbines in July 2022 (Table 1). Many of the flight trials occurred during morning hours when the wind conditions tended to be most compatible with flying the fixed-wing UAVs used in the study; however, limited winds allowed for extending the final 2022 sessions at the Goodnoe Hills later into early afternoon (at which point excessive summer heat precluded further flying).

The flight missions conducted at the Manzana site from January through March 2017 involved an initial, custom-built aircraft (AES Custom; Fig. 3A) flown by our first pilot. That aircraft crashed due to complicated flight conditions and was damaged enough to end the March flight trials. The August 2017 missions involved a different pilot and a new custom-built aircraft (AUV Custom; Fig. 3B). The Manzana missions resulted in a total of 1279 distinct, independent flight transects that DTBird should have been able to detect and were suited to quantifying the probability of detection (Table 1). DTBird detected 798 (62%) of those flight transects. Of the detected transects, 24 (3%) did not trigger a deterrent signal (i.e., were detection-only events), 191 (24%) triggered only a warning signal, 333 (42%) triggered only a dissuasion signal, and 250 (31%) triggered both deterrent signals.

At Goodnoe Hills, we attempted an initial round of flight trials in May 2021 with a new pilot team and aircraft, but this effort resulted in no useable data primarily due to incompatible flight conditions. We then conducted successful flight trials at three turbines on 2 d in early August 2021, involving mixed use of two UAVs (Clouds 1 [Fig. 3C] and Believer [Fig. 3D]). This flight-trial session was terminated prematurely when both aircraft suffered crashes that caused extensive damage. We conducted additional successful flight trials at four turbines on 4 d in late July 2022, involving an augmented piloting team and new UAVs (primarily a new Ranger [Fig. 3D], but also a Clouds 2 [Fig. 3C] similar to the previous model). The Goodnoe Hills missions resulted in 482 distinct, independent flight transects that DTBird should have been able to detect and were suited to quantifying the probability of detection (Table 1). DTBird detected 310 (63%) of these flight transects. Of the detected transects, 48 (15%) did not trigger a deterrent signal, 80 (26%) triggered only a warning signal, 138 (46%) triggered only a dissuasion signal, and 44 (14%) triggered both types of signals.

## DISCUSSION

Probability of Detection. The modeling results confirmed consistent performance of the primary – DTBird detection functions at the two study sites (64 66% probability of detection). The probability of detection modeling also provided insight concerning factors that influenced the probability of DTBird detecting an eagle-like UAV if it flew through the expected detection envelope calibrated for Golden Eagles. The limitation of this analysis was that, for flights that passed through the detection envelope but were not detected (false negatives), there were no reference points to use for precisely characterizing the flight, location, and environmental characteristics at the time of a specific DTBird event to use as covariates. Consequently, we focused attention on discerning the influences of only a select few metrics derived by using GIS tools to calculate minimum and average position metrics across all points along a given sample flight. Here it is also important to note that the collection of independent flight samples included primarily, but not exclusively, linear flights through the detection envelopes. Nevertheless, this relatively simple approach illustrated variability in the probability of detection through the day, likely related to the relative influence of solar position and intensity.

More importantly, the results emphasized that the probability of detection was highest when the target flew at moderate distances from the turbine (generally high with average flight distances of 80–160 m) through the midsection of the camera viewsheds (generally high with viewing angles from camera up to UAV of 25–40[] ). Conversely, the probability of detection averaged lower when the target flew either closer to or farther away from the camera or primarily within the lower or upper margins of the camera viewshed. These results are perhaps not surprising in suggesting that detection tends to be lower around the margins of the camera viewsheds and higher when a bird is flying at moderate distances from and in the center of a camera viewshed. The latter conditions are exactly when birds approaching a spinning turbine tend to be at greatest risk of entering the rotor-swept zone. However, especially hunting or displaying raptors such as Golden Eagles often make dynamic movements that can either rapidly drop them down from up high or pop them up from down low and quickly bring them into the rotor-swept zone at relatively close range. For this reason, poorer detection low-and-close or high-and-close to the turbine

could result in problematic interactions with little time for the deterrents to trigger and discourage continued closer passage before entering the collision risk zone. This may be a particularly acute issue in topographically complex landscapes where sudden pop-ups are common as eagles take advantage of orographic lift to contour hunt and surprise-attack prey. Moreover, this potential limitation may be exacerbated by DTBird not being capable of detecting moving objects against a landscape backdrop.

Modeling Response Distances. The average response distance for detection events (190 m) was longer than for dissuasion signals (176 m), as expected, but was considerably shorter than the 240-m theoretical maximum, calibrated detection distance. This result reflected that initial detections often occurred when the UAV: (1) flew in low and first entered the inverted-cone-shaped detection envelope from the underside at relatively close distances to the turbine (Fig. 2); (2) dropped down from on high through the DTBird blind-zone straight above the turbine and was not detected until already within the inner dissuasion-triggering zone (Fig. 2); or (3) simply was not detected until it flew closer to a camera with a more exposed profile and/or otherwise better exposure conditions. Greater-than-expected response distances also occurred but were comparatively uncommon.

Figure 10. GLMM predicted relationships between DTBird detection and deterrent-triggering response distances and the interactive influences of UAV roll angles (left and right wing dips) and pitch angles (nose up or down), as measured by UAV avionics during sampling flights.

A similar factor also contributed to the outcome for warning signals, where some initial triggers were expected to occur at distances of 100–170 m (Fig. 3); however, with the realm over which such warning signals could occur limited to less than one third of the area over which shorter detection distances could arise, the matching average detection and warning signal response distances were unexpected. This outcome may reflect that, despite mostly common triggering calibration, greater-than-expected warning-signal response distances were proportionately less common than greater-than-expected detection response distances. This could be considered a desirable result in that it means relevant targets were sometimes detected at greater than expected distances—increasing time for an effective deterrent response if needed—but unnecessary warning signals targeting extra-distant birds were constrained.

The average response distance for triggering a dissuasion signal (176 m) nearly matched the calibrated core-envelope trigger distance for that event type (170 m), whereas the expectation was for a lower average reflecting a mix of expected response distances of approximately 170 m across the coreenvelope surveillance area and 100 m in the outer, lower band of surveillance areas (Fig. 2). Instead, the observed outcome suggested that dissuasion signals

were triggered more often than expected at distances exceeding the calibrated trigger distances. This outcome also could be considered beneficially conservative in providing more time for an approaching bird to respond to a dissuasion signal; however, excessive triggering of especially the dissuasion signals may have adverse consequences for non-target wildlife, facility staff, or facility neighbors (H. T. Harvey & Associates 2018).

The modeling results illustrated notable random variation among turbines at the two study sites, and indicated that, given modeling of other random and fixed effects, the overall DTBird response distances tended to average marginally shorter at the Manzana study site compared to the Goodnoe Hills site. Reasons for this difference are uncertain, but it suggests that the overall targeting accuracy of the DTBird systems can vary slightly across different landscape settings, perhaps reflecting inherent differences in the overall visual clarity and complexity of different regional skies and landscape backdrops. DTBird does not reliably detect objects against a landscape backdrop, and topographic complexity sometimes intrudes within the camera viewsheds to limit detectability. In this case, the proximate and elevated backdrop of the Tehachapi Mountains may have complicated detectability at the Manzana site more than the comparatively wide-open, ridgetop skies at the Goodnoe Hills site.

The modeled variation in average response distances among the five distinct UAV models deployed in this study might have coarsely mimicked the kind of random variation that could be expected given eagles of different sizes and coloration. However, the nature of “morphological” variation among the UAVs was not well correlated with the specific features of age- or sexrelated variation that would pertain to actual eagles. In fact, some of the body-form variation among the UAVs (e.g., skinny, tubular hind torsos on two aircraft; Fig. 3) was more extreme than would be relevant among actual eagles and, therefore, might have led to greater differences in detection probabilities than would be true for actual eagles. Nevertheless, we think it is reasonable to expect that individual and age/sexrelated variation in plumage coloration and body size/wingspan among Golden Eagles (as well as Bald Eagles [Haliaeetus leucocephalus] and other large soaring raptors) could have a similar effect on DTBird’s probability of detection.

Response distances generally increased as cloud cover increased and averaged significantly longer once the cloud cover extended throughout the viewshed under relatively uniform overcast skies. This outcome is logical in suggesting that the

DTBird systems more readily detected the relatively dark eagle-like UAVs against relatively uniform high-contrast white or gray backgrounds than against less contrasting blue skies or highly dynamic partly cloudy skies. These tendencies also mimic the challenges faced by human observers scanning the skies for migrating raptors, where the presence of uniform cloud cover greatly increases the detectability of migrants passing overhead underneath the clouds (Bildstein et al. 2007).

Furthermore, across the UAV ground speeds documented in this study, DTBird’s targeting performance improved as the UAV travel rate from the perspective of the fixed-position cameras increased. Although not a particularly strong response, this result could reflect DTBird programming that emphasizes flight speed as among the criteria used to reduce false positive detections. The DTBird detection algorithm focuses on targeting objects that both fill enough image pixels to warrant targeting from an estimated distance perspective, and that it registers as moving in a manner that could be a flying bird.

We included in our modeling effort consideration of a suite of variables as potential indicators of variation in the exposure of UAV profiles to the cameras, where greater profile exposure was expected to increase the accuracy of DTBird targeting based on calibrated settings. Our hypothesis was that the more a UAV climbs or descends, pitches up or down in the wind, or rolls from side to side in the wind or while banking, the more the UAV profile should be exposed to the cameras and lead to more accurate targeting. Positive associations with wind speed and the interactive influence of roll and pitch angles confirmed this hypothesis. Insight regarding the interactive influence of pitch and roll angles was probably constrained compared to results that would be obtained by modeling the movements of real eagles. An eagle’s ability to undertake complicated in-flight maneuvers—such as steep pitch and roll dives—is far greater than could have been accomplished with the fixed-wing UAVs used in this study. This factor may limit the relevance of insights generated from the study. It is also likely, however, that modeling the movements of real eagles would only further emphasize the positive relationship between DTBird’s targeting responses and movement dynamics that increase exposure of an eagle’s—or UAV-surrogate’s—profile to the DTBird cameras.

We also considered in our modeling potential predictors relating to the positioning and intensity of solar irradiation impinging on the UAV in the direction of the cameras. Such predictors proved informative in an initial Manzana site-specific analysis but not

in an improved Goodnoe Hills site-specific analysis (H. T. Harvey & Associates unpubl. data) nor in the multi-site model presented here. Flying objects seen in the DTBird videos and targeted by the system routinely disappear when passing through major sunspots and high intensity solar insolation often increases the glare factor around such sunspots. In this case, however, we suspect that the combined-site dataset more effectively captured this effect in the refined relationship with sky backdrop/cloud cover. Specifically, situations where substantial sunspots obscured detectability were particularly prevalent under fair and partly cloudy skies, but were greatly diminished when cloud cover was more complete, especially once overcast skies prevailed. Hence, the relative prevalence of sunspots and glare patterns may have been a primary driver behind the apparent positive relationship between response distances and cloud cover illustrated in the multi-site model, to the exclusion of solar intensity or positioning proving to be of additional predictive value.

Study Limitations and Constraints. This investigation highlighted several flight metrics and environmental covariates that appeared to significantly influence DTBird’s detection and deterrent-triggering performance at the two study sites. It is important to acknowledge, however, that using eagle-like UAVs as surrogates for real eagles may have constrained the insights generated from the study. We think the fixed-wing UAVs we used in the study did a good job of mimicking the non-flapping soaring and sailing flights of eagles, but were limited by not having wings that flap and tuck in the manner used by eagles to accomplish certain maneuvers. The UAVs were also not capable of undertaking steep dive-and-roll or “roller-coaster” type display maneuvers that Golden Eagles sometimes make in pursuing prey or as part of their territorial behavior (Katzner et al. 2020). The degree to which moredynamic wing action and flight maneuvers could alter the apparent targeting performance of DTBird or similar detection systems is uncertain. Wing flapping undoubtedly exposes more of a bird’s profile to the cameras, at least intermittently; however, wing tucking does the opposite.

Regulatory concerns about possible conflicts between UAVs and in situ eagles both limited where we were able to conduct this UAV-based research (high-density eagle locations prohibited by the US Fish and Wildlife Service) and influenced implementation of the UAV flight trials at the selected study sites. During the flight trials we conducted, we experienced only two brief encounters between our UAVs and in situ eagles, both involving young

subadult Golden Eagles in California that initially appeared curious but flew away as soon as the pilot revved the UAV motor to move away from the eagles. In contrast, although both Golden Eagles and Bald Eagles were occasionally present on the Goodnoe Hills ridgeline while we were conducting flight trials, none required diverting a UAV to avoid conflict.

Incompatible weather and wind conditions greatly constrained our efforts to use fixed-wing UAVs as eagle surrogates. In general, the efficacy of using UAVs as a sampling tool to mimic large raptors at wind facilities will always be limited due to their inability to tolerate flying in the strong, turbulent winds characteristic of many facilities. Turbulent and strong winds caused three of four fatal UAV crashes in this study; wind speeds above approximately 8–10 m/sec precluded safe operations. Fixed-wing UAVs also cannot fly when there is notable moisture in the air from fog, low clouds, or precipitation, because moisture can be drawn directly into the avionics. Excessive heat also restricts UAV operations by adversely affecting the control hardware and radio communications. Each of these factors constrained our operations and, combined with limitations pertaining to the cost and logistical aspects of accessing remote field sites, ultimately reduced our sampling effort well below the intended design for this research. The greatest limitation of the dataset is not having sampled well under broader ranges of diel timing and seasonal environmental conditions. This limits the breadth of confident insight from the study regarding the influence on detectability of variable sky conditions and solar insolation, for example. Nevertheless, the overall effort across the two field sites provided sufficient data to yield important insight about DTBird’s performance in two different landscapes, and how salient flight characteristics and environmental covariates influenced DTBird’s performance in detecting eagle surrogates and triggering deterrence signals compared to calibrated system settings.

Having four UAVs suffer irreparable damage resulted in our flying a greater diversity of models than initially anticipated, which may have mimicked some of the variability in DTBird performance that would likely occur given eagles of various sizes and color patterns. Our original study design did not anticipate achieving such an objective, but with hindsight we recommend that similar, future research incorporate from the outset a fleet of several UAVs that all effectively mimic the focal species of interest but vary in their overall morphology in a manner consistent with expected intraspecies variation. Flight trials would then be conducted while rotating use of the

different models among sessions. Maintaining a fleet of aircraft that are always on-hand would also provide critical redundancy in case of aircraft failure/damage.

If efforts to use UAVs as bird mimics are considered for similar future studies, some of the new robotic birds available today that are 3D printed to closely resemble specific birds and fly with moveable wings (e.g., see https://aeriumanalytics.com/robird and https://lentinklab.com/aerial-robot-design) should be considered, as long as the flapping rate effectively mimics that of the focal bird species. A robotic bird with quick wingbeats that flaps all the time to stay aloft would not be a good mimic for eagles, because eagles often spend most of their time in nonflapping soaring and sailing flight, rather than using powered flight (e.g., see Katzner et al. 2020). In addition, although multi-rotor drones of sufficient size are more stable in flight, can be flown with moisture in the air, and likely could withstand flying at higher wind speeds and under more turbulent conditions, they cannot effectively mimic the basic body and wing form of an eagle. Therefore, any insights generated about relative detectability would have to be further qualified as only marginally applicable to detecting real birds. Testing detection systems using flights of live eagles also makes logical sense, but is confounded by challenges orchestrating diverse flights of falconry eagles or having numerous wild eagles tagged with high-resolution GPS devices closely flying around several DTBird-equipped turbines (but see May et al. 2012).

It is important to recognize that using eagle-like UAV surrogates as a testing tool will not work effectively if the camera resolution is good enough and programming of the detection system is sophisticated enough to automatically identify target birds and exclude tracking of nontarget birds and other inanimate objects (e.g., see McClure et al. 2021). The DTBird detection algorithms do accomplish some such filtering to reduce targeting of commercial airplanes and insects, for example, but not to a degree sufficient to preclude effective use of fixedwing UAVs to coarsely mimic eagles. The results presented here, combined with other multi-faceted results from our overall DTBird research program (see Felton et al. 2024), have and will support improvements to the DTBird detection system that may eventually limit the applicability of using UAVs as a relevant testing tool. Nevertheless, UAVs can be an efficient and effective tool for conducting initial evaluations and coarse-scale refining of various imaging and detection systems designed to detect flying animals (e.g., visual, radar, and thermal; H. T. Harvey & Associates unpubl. data). Further, robotic

bird-like UAVs eventually may serve as much better eagle surrogates for testing more advanced detection systems.

UAVs provided a standardized approach to test the ability of the DTBird detection and deterrenttriggering modules to operate as intended (i.e., to effectively detect targets and trigger warning and dissuasion signals when they fly within the detection envelope). Testing the efficacy of the DTBird system to minimize risks to eagles requires observations of wild-eagle behavioral responses, but evaluating the overall performance of the DTBird system requires understanding not only the system’s ability to detect eagles and trigger the deterrents, but also to elicit a response. We will address eagle behavioral responses to the DTBird system in an upcoming manuscript; and future journal articles will present other related research findings and ultimately an overarching assessment of DTBird’s effectiveness in reducing collision risk for Golden Eagles and other large soaring raptors (see Felton et al. 2024 for previews).

title: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles Used to Assess Performance of Automated Detection and Audio Deterrent System for Reducing Wind-Turbine Collison Risk for Golden Eagles
abstract: DTBird is an automated detection and audio deterrent system designed to discourage birds from approaching spinning wind turbines. With Golden Eagles (Aquila chrysaetos) the focal species of interest, we evaluated DTBird’s performance at two commercial facilities, one situated in a desert landscape in California, USA (Manzana site), and the other in a temperate grassland/scrub landscape on a ridgeline above the Columbia River in Washington, USA (Goodnoe Hills site). To evaluate DTBird’s detection and deterrent-triggering functions, we used fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) as eagle surrogates in experimental flight trials, involving planned transect arrays that supported evaluating DTBird responses within a 240-m-radius expected maximum, hemispheric detection envelope. We quantified the probability of detection and used logistic regression to evaluate the influence of several predictors. We also built a general linear mixed-effects model (GLMM) to evaluate the influence of several environmental covariates and flight metrics on DTBird detection and deterrent-triggering response distances. The estimated probability of detection was similar at the two sites (64–66%), increased from morning through afternoon (effects of sun positioning), and was highest when the target flew at moderate distances from the turbine through the midsection of the camera viewsheds. The GLMM analysis confirmed modest variation relating to the five distinct UAV models used, possibly mimicking variation that would apply to eagles of variable size and coloration. The analysis also demonstrated that response distances averaged marginally shorter at the Manzana site and increased (suggesting improved detectability) under uniform cloud cover and as the UAV travel rate and exposure of the UAV profile to the cameras increased. Our experience also emphasized that effective use of foam-bodied, fixed-wing UAVs as eagle surrogates at wind facilities can be strongly limited by complicated topography that restricts centralized flight operations; intervening obstacles such as overhead powerlines that restrict automated flight missions; and excessive wind, inclement weather, and rough landing conditions around many turbines that can easily lead to UAV crashes and damage. Using eagle-like UAVs with immobile wings as eagle surrogates also might have constrained the insights generated from the study. Nevertheless, the indicated relationships can help future system users understand the environmental conditions in which DTBird and similar automated systems are likely to perform best and other factors that can substantially influence the targeting accuracy of such systems.

## Unmanned Aerial Vehicles Used to Assess Performance of Automated Detection and Audio Deterrent System for Reducing Wind-Turbine Collison Risk for Golden Eagles

**Article** _in_ Journal of Raptor Research · January 2025 DOI: 10.3356/jrr2448

Journal of Raptor Research 59(1):jrr2448 doi: 10.3356/jrr2448  2025 The Raptor Research Foundation, Inc.

## Unmanned Aerial Vehicles Used to Assess Performance of Automated Detection and Audio Deterrent System for Reducing Wind-Turbine Collision Risk for Golden Eagles

Jeff P. Smith ,[1][*] Stephanie R. Schneider,[1] Jeff A. Zirpoli,[2][†] Scott B. Terrill,[1] Shilo K. Felton,[3] and Taber D. Allison[3]

- 1H. T. Harvey & Associates, 720 University Avenue, Suite 200, Los Gatos, CA 95032 USA

2H. T. Harvey & Associates, 8080 N. Palm Avenue, Suite 2053, Fresno, CA 93711 USA

3Renewable Energy Wildlife Institute, 700 12th Street, NW Suite 700, Washington, DC 20005 USA

ABSTRACT.—DTBird is an automated detection and audio deterrent system designed to discourage birds from approaching spinning wind turbines. With Golden Eagles (Aquila chrysaetos) the focal species of interest, we evaluated DTBird’s performance at two commercial facilities, one situated in a desert landscape in California, USA (Manzana site), and the other in a temperate grassland/scrub landscape on a ridgeline above the Columbia River in Washington, USA (Goodnoe Hills site). To evaluate DTBird’s detection and deterrent-triggering functions, we used fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) as eagle surrogates in experimental flight trials, involving planned transect arrays that supported evaluating DTBird responses within a 240-m-radius expected maximum, hemispheric detection envelope. We quantified the probability of detection and used logistic regression to evaluate the influence of several predictors. We also built a general linear mixed-effects model (GLMM) to evaluate the influence of several environmental covariates and flight metrics on DTBird detection and deterrent-triggering response distances. The estimated probability of detection was similar at the two sites (64–66%), increased from morning through afternoon (effects of sun positioning), and was highest when the target flew at moderate distances from the turbine through the midsection of the camera viewsheds. The GLMM analysis confirmed modest variation relating to the five distinct UAV models used, possibly mimicking variation that would apply to eagles of variable size and coloration. The analysis also demonstrated that response distances averaged marginally shorter at the Manzana site and increased (suggesting improved detectability) under uniform cloud cover and as the UAV travel rate and exposure of the UAV profile to the cameras increased. Our experience also emphasized that effective use of foam-bodied, fixed-wing UAVs as eagle surrogates at wind facilities can be strongly limited by complicated topography that restricts centralized flight operations; intervening obstacles such as overhead powerlines that restrict automated flight missions; and excessive wind, inclement weather, and rough landing conditions around many turbines that can easily lead to UAV crashes and damage. Using eagle-like UAVs with immobile wings as eagle surrogates also might have constrained the insights generated from the study. Nevertheless, the indicated relationships can help future system users understand the environmental conditions in which DTBird and similar automated systems are likely to perform best and other factors that can substantially influence the targeting accuracy of such systems.

KEY WORDS: avian deterrence technology; collision risk reduction; DTBird; impact minimization technology; mitigation; probability of detection; UAVs as eagle surrogates; wind energy.

RESUMEN.—DTBird[®] es un sistema de detección automática y disuasión sonora diseñado para desalentar a las aves de acercarse a las turbinas eólicas en movimiento. Considerando a Aquila chrysaetos como la especie de interés, evaluamos el desempeño de DTBird en dos instalaciones comerciales localizadas en un paisaje desértico de California y en un paisaje de pastizal/arbustos templados en la cima de un cordón montañoso que bordea el río Columbia en Washington. Para evaluar las funciones de detección y activación de disuasión de DTBird, usamos vehículos aéreos no tripulados (VANT) de ala fija como sustitutos de las águilas en ensayos de vuelo experimentales, utilizando esquemas de transectos previamente planificados que permitieran la evaluación de las respuestas de DTBird dentro de un radio máximo esperado de 240 metros en un área de detección hemisférica. Cuantificamos la probabilidad de detección y usamos regresión logística para evaluar la influencia de varios predictores. También construimos un modelo de efectos mixtos lineales generales (MEMLG) para evaluar la influencia de varias covariables ambientales y métricas de vuelo en las distancias de detección y activación de disuasión de DTBird. La probabilidad de detección estimada fue similar en los dos sitios (64-66%), aumentó de la mañana a la tarde (efectos de la posición del sol) y fue mayor cuando el objetivo volaba a distancias moderadas de la turbina a través de la sección media de los campos de visión de la cámara. El análisis MEMLG confirmó una variación moderada relacionada con los cinco modelos distintos de VANT utilizados, posiblemente imitando una variación que podría aplicarse a águilas de tamaño y coloración variables. El análisis también demostró que las distancias de respuesta fueron ligeramente más cortas en el sitio de Manzana y aumentaron (sugiriendo una mejor detectabilidad) bajo una cobertura de nubes uniforme y a medida que la velocidad de desplazamiento del VANT y la exposición de su perfil a las cámaras aumentaban. Nuestra experiencia también destacó que el uso efectivo de VANTs de cuerpo de espuma y ala fija como sustitutos de A. chrysaetos en instalaciones eólicas puede verse fuertemente limitado por una topografía complicada que restringe las operaciones de vuelo centralizadas; por obstáculos intermedios como líneas eléctricas que restringen las misiones de vuelo automatizadas; y por viento excesivo, condiciones climáticas adversas y condiciones de aterrizaje difíciles alrededor de muchas turbinas, que pueden llevar fácilmente a accidentes y daños en los VANT. El uso de VANTs con alas inmóviles como sustitutos de las águilas también podría haber limitado las conclusiones generadas en el estudio. No obstante, las relaciones indicadas pueden ayudar a los futuros usuarios del sistema a comprender las condiciones ambientales en las que DTBird y sistemas automáticos similares son más efectivos y otros factores que pueden influir sustancialmente en la precisión del sistema.

## INTRODUCTION

Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), also commonly known as drones, are increasingly being used for a variety of scientific survey, monitoring, and assessment purposes (Jones et al. 2012, Chabot and Bird 2015, Hodgson et al. 2016, Brinkman and Garcelon 2020). This includes robotic birds specifically developed to mimic certain kinds of raptors, including propulsion with flapping wings (e.g., see https:// aeriumanalytics.com/robird). Radio-controlled UAVs are also being used for practical applications such as hazing birds to reduce consumption of livestock feed, agricultural crops, and aquaculture products, similar to how falconry birds are sometimes used (Rhoades et al. 2019, Bhusal 2020, Egan et al. 2023). More recently, interest has grown around using UAVs to test human observers and especially automated detection systems designed to monitor

activity and trigger technological responses that reduce collision risk for birds of conservation concern around operating wind turbines (H. T. Harvey & Associates 2018). Herein we describe research where we used fixed-wing UAVs designed to coarsely mimic Golden Eagles (Aquila chrysaetos) to evaluate performance of the DTBird automated detection and audio deterrence system (Liquen Consultoría Ambiental, S.L., Madrid, Spain; see https://dtbird. com) installed at two onshore commercial windenergy facilities in the western United States.

This research was part of a multi-faceted, multiyear effort designed to quantify the effectiveness of turbine-mounted DTBird systems as a measure to reduce collision risk for Golden Eagles and other large raptors around spinning turbines (for comprehensive technical reports see H. T. Harvey & Associates 2018 [California pilot study] and Felton et al. 2024 [final multi-site report]). The overall

goal of the work was to facilitate consideration of the technology by the US Fish and Wildlife Service as a best management practice under the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act (16 USC §668–668d), as a minimization measure for take permits or habitat conservation plans, or as an adaptive management measure. Currently, DTBird and complementary DTBat systems have been installed at more than 90 wind farms across 16 countries in Europe, Asia, and North America (see https://www.dtbird.com). Previous DTBird pilot studies conducted in Europe are represented in May et al. (2012; relatively extensive study focused on GPS-tracked White-tailed Eagles [Haliaeetus albicilla] in Norway), Hanagasioglu et al. (2015; limited single-turbine assessment in Switzerland), and Litsgård et al. (2016; limited single-turbine assessment in Sweden). Our study represents the first extensive effort to evaluate the DTBird detection and audio deterrent system in North America, including novel use of UAVs as a tool to help evaluate performance of the detection and deterrent-triggering components of the system.

Focusing on the UAV-based assessments within the broader multi-faceted project, our objectives in this study were to (1) use fixed-wing UAVs as surrogates for Golden Eagles at two commercial wind-energy facilities in distinctly different landscapes to quantify the probability of detection for the evaluated system, and (2) model DTBird’s detection and deterrent-triggering response distances in relation to a variety of flight characteristics and environmental covariates. We also highlight some of the key pitfalls and limitations we encountered during this research, and outline guidance for potential future applications of UAV technology for similar purposes.

## METHODS

Study Sites and DTBird Installations. We conducted this research at the Manzana Wind Power Project in southern California, operated by Avangrid Renewables since 2012, and the Goodnoe Hills Wind Farm in south-central Washington, operated by PacifiCorp since 2008. The Manzana facility comprised 126 1.5-MW General Electric turbines with a hub height of 65 m and a rotor-swept diameter of 82.5 m. The Goodnoe Hills facility comprised 48 2.2-MW Vestas turbines with a hub height of 87 m and a rotor-swept diameter of 110 m.

The Manzana facility is located in the southwestern foothills of the Tehachapi Mountains within the westernmost extension of the Mojave Desert (Fig. 1). The landscape is a gradually sloping alluvial fan descending from foothill topography through a

mostly flat plain incised by dry desert washes, with desert-scrub, grassland, and sparse woodland (i.e., Juniperus spp., Yucca brevifolia, and Pinus-Quercus spp.) vegetation typical of the upper Mojave Desert region. Seven DTBird systems (DTBirdV4D4 Model 2020) were installed in strategic locations (pertaining to logistical feasibility/practicality and coarsescale habitat representation) at this facility to support this research (H. T. Harvey & Associates 2018, Felton et al. 2024).

The Goodnoe Hills facility is located atop an eastwest ridgeline that runs along the northern flank of the Columbia River (Fig. 1). The rolling-hills ridgeline topography descends steeply to the south approximately 610 m to the river and descends more gradually to the north approximately 500 m down into Rock Creek Canyon and associated riparian corridors. The project area is dominated by a mosaic of grazed grassland and shrubsteppe, with inclusions of pine-oak woodlands (Pinus ponderosa and Quercus garryana) on north-facing slopes. Fourteen DTBird systems (DTBirdV4D8 Model 2020) were installed around the perimeter of this facility to support this research; however, the operational functionality of these systems varied during the 2-yr study at this site (Felton et al. 2024).

DTBird System Operation. Each DTBird monitoring system comprised four video cameras (6megapixel resolution) installed on the turbine tower approximately 5 m off the ground. The four cameras were oriented in approximately cardinal directions and at an angle of 14[] above horizontal to focus most effectively on the rotor-swept zone of the relevant turbine. H. T. Harvey & Associates (2018) provides a comprehensive description of how the DTBird detection and deterrent-triggering systems work, along with detailed graphical illustrations of the expected camera viewsheds and deterrent-triggering zones.

In brief, each DTBird automated video system surveils the sky around an individual turbine through daylight hours (as set by the operator) for moving objects that qualify as a target of interest based on calibrations for focal species of interest. DTBird does not classify or enumerate targets, may target multiple objects simultaneously, and does not track individual objects—it simply repeatedly registers individual events involving objects that meet the calibrated targeting criteria and stores video clips of those events. Analysts must subsequently review event records and video clips stored in the system’s online digital analysis platform (DAP) to classify and enumerate the detected targets, which may be targeted birds or false

DTBird systems are calibrated to target objects of a specified size range and, if a system registers that the turbine rotor is actively spinning at $2 rotations per minute (rpm), to trigger subsequent deterrent signals when the system estimates that a targeted object is within a specified distance from the turbine. Detection and trigger distances are determined based on pre-programmed criteria projecting how many image pixels a bird of the specified size is expected to fill at specific distances. The Manzana and Goodnoe Hills systems were calibrated to target Golden Eagles with a wingspan of 2.1–2.3 m, which translated to targeting objects that met specified criteria at an expected maximum line-of-sight (LoS) distance from the turbine of approximately 240 m (Fig. 2). Once an object was targeted and a new detection record was initiated at a spinning turbine, the system generally triggered an initial warning signal (i.e., a relatively benign artificial whistle-whoop signal designed to initially draw the bird’s attention) if it registered that a targeted object moved within 170–240 m of the turbine. – If a targeted object moved within 100 170 m, the system generally triggered a dissuasion signal (i.e., a very loud, more raucous/aggressive series of mechanical

sounds designed to actively discourage the bird from further approach). However, trigger distances also varied depending on the flight altitude and preconceived collision risk, progressively decreasing with decreasing flight altitude as the risk of exposure to the rotor-swept zone theoretically diminished (lower sweep at 24 m and 32 m above ground at Manzana and Goodnoe Hills, respectively; Fig. 2). This configuration meant that targets approaching at low altitudes were detected only at relatively close range and immediately triggered a dissuasion signal without a preceding warning signal.

When a turbine-specific DTBird system first detected a targeted object via any of its four cameras, it created a new event record in the DAP and recorded a timestamp for the initial detection event along with other limited data. If a bird subsequently or simultaneously triggered one or both deterrent signals while targeted in any of the four cameras, information was added to the same DAP event record to document the unique timestamps and signal durations for each deterrent-triggering event. There must have been no objects targeted for at least 26 sec in any of the cameras before a given DTBird system could initiate a new independent detection event record. UAV Flight Trials. We flew two UAVs during the Manzana flight trials and four other UAVs during the Goodnoe Hills flight trials (Fig. 3). All were similar in being fixed-wing plastic/foam-bodied models built using commercially available body kits and customized to withstand landing on rough surfaces. Each UAV incorporated a nose-cone video camera and included high-end avionics that provided data on flight dynamics, wind speed, and GPS tracking – with high spatial (1 2 m) and temporal (many times per second) resolution. The aircraft were not built specifically to mimic the body form of a Golden Eagle, but their wingspans of approximately 2 m, body lengths of approximately 1 m, and masses with a full battery load of approximately 3 kg were comparable to that of an eagle and they were painted with brownish coloration to coarsely resemble a Golden Eagle. The aircraft differed in overall size, body

morphology, and coloration, which we postulated could coarsely mimic morphological variation seen among individual eagles of different ages and sexes. That said, variability in the UAVs used unexpectedly stemmed from having to replace four of the six aircraft following crashes that resulted in irreparable damage, and there was no common usage of individual UAVs between the two study sites.

Our study plans for both facilities called for conducting robust suites of UAV flight trials at all (Manzana) or a representative selection of (Goodnoe Hills) DTBird installations, repeated across different seasons with variable sky cover and flight conditions. In the end, complicated flight conditions for flying light-bodied, fixed-wing UAVs and unexpected calamities hindered achieving this objective. The key commonality at the two study sites was that we flew primarily preplanned linear transects orchestrated as automated, multi-transect flight missions at selected DTBird-equipped turbines, with the goal of achieving representative sampling of the hemispheric, 240-m-radius expected detection envelopes around the sampled DTBird installations (Fig. 4).

We then strategically packaged collections of pre-delineated, linear transects to orchestrate efficient, single battery-powered (30– 40 min duration), automated flight missions, which were often manually augmented with several lowaltitude passes as supplemental battery life allowed. The avionics settings and automated flight-control parameters were set so that the UAVs generally flew near the lower end of possible travel speeds to better mimic average eagle flight speeds and behaviors, although such controls still translated to appropriately rapid flight speeds during descending flights and when the UAV was pushed by a strong tailwind. Measured UAV flight speeds relative to the ground during the study ranged from 0.4–114.1 km/hr (mean 6 SD: 58.0 6 15.5 km/hr). In comparison, Golden Eagle flight speeds while soaring and gliding can range from negligible to as much as 190 km/h, with vertical dives sometimes reaching more than 200 km/hr (Katzner et al. 2020).

At both sites we sought to conduct at least halfday flight-trial sessions, each involving multiple automated flight missions, at several representative DTBird-equipped turbines where the operational

conditions allowed for safely launching and landing the aircraft near the focal turbine, the topography was compatible with maintaining eye contact and radio control with the aircraft at all times, and the flight arena included minimal complications caused by elevated obstacles besides the focal turbine and usually one other adjacent turbine (both curtailed during all relevant flight trials). All seven Manzana setups provided such compatible circumstances, whereas several of the Goodnoe Hills setups did not. The Goodnoe Hills systems were installed to support a multi-year, multi-faceted study (Felton et al. 2024). As such, the DTBird turbines were selected to support multiple objectives (i.e., encompass representative eagle activity and provide a well-spaced perimeter array), and included some locations that were not compatible with conducting safe and effective UAV flight trials.

All flights were conducted using professional pilots that held remote pilot airman certificates with small unmanned aircraft (UAS) ratings issued by the Federal Aviation Administration (2020) to support commercial UAV operations. The piloting team used Mission Planner software (ArduPilot Dev Team 2021) on a laptop with radio communication to the UAV to orchestrate each automated mission and receive data transmitted from the aircraft. During all flight trials, the field team comprised: (a) a licensed pilot operating the UAV controller, (b) a “laptop pilot” operating Mission Planner to implement the automated missions and communicate navigational guidance and battery awareness to the pilot, and (c) an experienced raptor biologist (JPS) responsible for detecting in situ raptors and coordinating avoidance of potentially problematic encounters with the UAV.

Each pre-delineated, linear flight transect began and ended 100-m LoS distance beyond the projected 240-m detection envelope to support the possibility of extra-limital detections. Once the DTBird system targeted an object and created a new detection record in the DAP, no new detection record could be created until no additional targeting had occurred for at least 26 sec. Accordingly, to generate independent transect

samples for evaluating the probability of detection and the DTBird system’s response characteristics, the automated flight missions included 30-sec loiter periods between each delineated transect at one of 5–6 preselected, safe destinations located 500 m from the relevant study turbine. To supplement the arrays of predefined linear transects, we manually flew variable numbers of low-altitude transects at each site. During these flights, the pilot flew the UAV toward the turbine below the expected inverted-cone detection range (Fig. 4) and then brought it up into the detection range relatively close to the turbine using both linear and sometimes circling ascents. Data Processing. Each UAV was equipped with avionics that recorded for each flight myriad GPS position, ground and air speed, flight trajectory, and other flight metrics many times per second with high spatial accuracy. These data were automatically transmitted during the flights to the control laptop and could be

extracted directly from the avionics units post-flight. The resulting output from each individual flight was a continuous stream of nonparsed data, which we translated to a usable format using a customized dataextraction program (Fernie 2012). The overall translation, extraction, and formatting process followed the detailed procedures and protocols described in H. T. Harvey & Associates (2018). Once the avionics data were extracted and formatted, we matched these data with verified DTBird UAV detection and deterrenttriggering event records based on common timestamps with 1-sec resolution. We then extracted all individually matched flight transects and event records, and combined data from the two study sites to compose the dataset we used to model the response-distance performance characteristics of the DTBird detection and deterrent-triggering functions.

Using the flight-trial data to quantify the probability of DTBird detecting an eagle-surrogate UAV required further processing of the continuous tracking data from each multi-transect flight mission into distinct, independent sample transects. In brief, this involved using ArcGIS 3D Analyst to clip out all tracking data related to loiter-point activity and segment the remaining data into individual, independent flight paths/transects suited to evaluating the probability of detection. Specifically, GIS analysts used 3D Analyst to develop dome-shaped clipping masks and exclude all tracking data beyond 340 m LoS distance from the focal turbine center point at 4–5 m above ground level (i.e., the approximate position of the DTBird cameras on the turbine tower). This clipping distance encompassed the farthest DTBird detections but excluded all loiter tracking, which then allowed for isolating individual sampling flights.

Probability of Detection. To generate estimates of the probability of detecting an eagle-like UAV, we classified each independent flight transect as detected or not detected by the relevant DTBird system, and then calculated the proportions of flight transects in each category at each sampled turbine. The grand-average of the proportions detected at each turbine then represented overall site-specific estimates of the probability of detecting an eagle-like UAV that passed within the expected 240-m maximum detection range of the calibrated DTBird systems.

To generate additional insight about patterns of variability in the probability of detection, we conducted a logistic regression analysis using Systat 13.2.01 (Systat Software, Inc., San Jose, CA). Detected or not detected was the binary response variable, which we evaluated in relation to Site as a categorical predictor, Hour of the Day, and three UAV position metrics: average

Detection Angle, minimum LoS Distance, and average Exposure Direction. (See Supplemental Material S1 for detailed descriptions of the analyzed variables and the full model structure.) To select a final model, we evaluated representative candidate models based on Akaike’s Information Criterion (AIC) scores, log-likelihood ratio chi-square tests, individual parameter tests, and Nagelkerke pseudo-R[2] values (Nagelkerke 1991) to identify a final model given the predictors considered, and to evaluate the relative influences of various predictors on the probability of detection.

Analyzing DTBird’s Response Performance. We developed generalized linear mixed-effect models (GLMMs) to assess the influences of various factors on DTBird’s detection and deterrent-triggering performance. The GLMM statistical framework was particularly suited to analyzing this dataset, because it involved various dependencies and sources of variability. The primary response variable was the LoS distance from the closest DTBird camera at which the UAV was detected or a deterrent event was triggered. This is a metric of fundamental importance because it reflects how early the system identified a potential collision threat and, where relevant, triggered a deterrent signal. The operative assumption was that greater response distances could be interpreted as reflecting an improved detection or triggering response, in that earlier (more distant) detection and targeting was expected to provide more time for the deterrents to alter a target bird’s behavior before the risk of collision became acute. Using 3D Analyst measuring tools, we calculated LoS distances based on the UAV GPS coordinates at the time of each relevant DTBird event. Flight transects included in these analyses were necessarily limited to those that triggered a relevant DTBird response. To fit the response-distance data, we constructed GLMMs to evaluate the influence of various potential random- and fixed-effect predictors hypothesized to influence the response distances. We implemented the models using the lme4 package in R (R Core Team 2023; function lmer, Bates et al. 2015), with a Gaussian distribution and an identity link function.

The final multi-site analysis presented here benefited from insights gained from initial site-specific analyses conducted for the two study sites (e.g., see H. T. Harvey & Associates 2018). Our initial GLMMs included several fixed effects, including environmental variables (sky condition, cloud cover, and light conditions), UAV flight metrics (speed, altitude, and orientation), and DTBird system configurations (camera settings and operational parameters). To account for inherent variations in our experimental setup, we also incorporated random effects for

turbine location and UAV model nested within sites. (See Supplemental Material S2 for detailed descriptions of the full suite of variables considered as the full model for this analysis.) After fitting the full model, we used diagnostic tests to determine if the model violated any GLMM assumptions (Zuur et al. 2009, Wood 2017) using the R package DHARMa (Hartig 2021). Along with residual diagnostics, we evaluated potential combinations of predictors for indications of collinearity, and specifically avoided variable combinations that produced variance inflation factors (VIFs) greater than 5 (Hair et al. 1998, Zuur et al. 2010).

We identified the subset of predictors that best explained variation in the observed response distances via stepwise model selection using the step function in R’s base stats package and following the GLMM model selection guidance of Zuur et al. (2009). This stepwise-selection was done in combination with ANOVA-based and likelihood-ratio test comparisons of nested candidate models and evaluation of AIC scores, Nakagawa pseudo-R[2] values (Nakagawa et al. 2017), and residual plots to select the best model. In considering candidate models, we evaluated only models that met the assumptions of GLMMs. Given the considerable number of predictors and unbalanced categorical factors with some groups having relatively small sample sizes, we used AIC corrected for small sample sizes (AICc) to compare candidate models and avoid overfitting. We generated graphics resulting from the best model using siPlot (Ludecke€ 2023) and emmeans (Length 2023), both of which rely on ggplot2 (Wickham 2016). In discussing the significance of statistical results, we label results with P  0.01 as highly significant, 0.01 , P  0.05 as significant, and 0.05 , P  0.10 as marginally significant.

## RESULTS

Sampling Results. We conducted UAV flight trials at all seven Manzana DTBird installations, with sessions occurring from January through August in 2017 (most concentrated in August), at three Goodnoe Hills DTBird turbines in August 2021, and at four Goodnoe Hills turbines in July 2022 (Table 1). Many of the flight trials occurred during morning hours when the wind conditions tended to be most compatible with flying the fixed-wing UAVs used in the study; however, limited winds allowed for extending the final 2022 sessions at the Goodnoe Hills later into early afternoon (at which point excessive summer heat precluded further flying).

The flight missions conducted at the Manzana site from January through March 2017 involved an initial, custom-built aircraft (AES Custom; Fig. 3A) flown by our first pilot. That aircraft crashed due to complicated flight conditions and was damaged enough to end the March flight trials. The August 2017 missions involved a different pilot and a new custom-built aircraft (AUV Custom; Fig. 3B). The Manzana missions resulted in a total of 1279 distinct, independent flight transects that DTBird should have been able to detect and were suited to quantifying the probability of detection (Table 1). DTBird detected 798 (62%) of those flight transects. Of the detected transects, 24 (3%) did not trigger a deterrent signal (i.e., were detection-only events), 191 (24%) triggered only a warning signal, 333 (42%) triggered only a dissuasion signal, and 250 (31%) triggered both deterrent signals.

At Goodnoe Hills, we attempted an initial round of flight trials in May 2021 with a new pilot team and aircraft, but this effort resulted in no useable data primarily due to incompatible flight conditions. We then conducted successful flight trials at three turbines on 2 d in early August 2021, involving mixed use of two UAVs (Clouds 1 [Fig. 3C] and Believer [Fig. 3D]). This flight-trial session was terminated prematurely when both aircraft suffered crashes that caused extensive damage. We conducted additional successful flight trials at four turbines on 4 d in late July 2022, involving an augmented piloting team and new UAVs (primarily a new Ranger [Fig. 3D], but also a Clouds 2 [Fig. 3C] similar to the previous model). The Goodnoe Hills missions resulted in 482 distinct, independent flight transects that DTBird should have been able to detect and were suited to quantifying the probability of detection (Table 1). ## DISCUSSION

Probability of Detection. The modeling results confirmed consistent performance of the primary – DTBird detection functions at the two study sites (64 66% probability of detection). The probability of detection modeling also provided insight concerning factors that influenced the probability of DTBird detecting an eagle-like UAV if it flew through the expected detection envelope calibrated for Golden Eagles. The limitation of this analysis was that, for flights that passed through the detection envelope but were not detected (false negatives), there were no reference points to use for precisely characterizing the flight, location, and environmental characteristics at the time of a specific DTBird event to use as covariates. Consequently, we focused attention on discerning the influences of only a select few metrics derived by using GIS tools to calculate minimum and average position metrics across all points along a given sample flight. Here it is also important to note that the collection of independent flight samples included primarily, but not exclusively, linear flights through the detection envelopes. Nevertheless, this relatively simple approach illustrated variability in the probability of detection through the day, likely related to the relative influence of solar position and intensity.

More importantly, the results emphasized that the probability of detection was highest when the target flew at moderate distances from the turbine (generally high with average flight distances of 80–160 m) through the midsection of the camera viewsheds (generally high with viewing angles from camera up to UAV of 25–40[] ). Conversely, the probability of detection averaged lower when the target flew either closer to or farther away from the camera or primarily within the lower or upper margins of the camera viewshed. These results are perhaps not surprising in suggesting that detection tends to be lower around the margins of the camera viewsheds and higher when a bird is flying at moderate distances from and in the center of a camera viewshed. The latter conditions are exactly when birds approaching a spinning turbine tend to be at greatest risk of entering the rotor-swept zone. However, especially hunting or displaying raptors such as Golden Eagles often make dynamic movements that can either rapidly drop them down from up high or pop them up from down low and quickly bring them into the rotor-swept zone at relatively close range. For this reason, poorer detection low-and-close or high-and-close to the turbine

This may be a particularly acute issue in topographically complex landscapes where sudden pop-ups are common as eagles take advantage of orographic lift to contour hunt and surprise-attack prey. Moreover, this potential limitation may be exacerbated by DTBird not being capable of detecting moving objects against a landscape backdrop.

Modeling Response Distances. The average response distance for detection events (190 m) was longer than for dissuasion signals (176 m), as expected, but was considerably shorter than the 240-m theoretical maximum, calibrated detection distance. This result reflected that initial detections often occurred when the UAV: (1) flew in low and first entered the inverted-cone-shaped detection envelope from the underside at relatively close distances to the turbine (Fig. 2); (2) dropped down from on high through the DTBird blind-zone straight above the turbine and was not detected until already within the inner dissuasion-triggering zone (Fig. 2); or (3) simply was not detected until it flew closer to a camera with a more exposed profile and/or otherwise better exposure conditions. Greater-than-expected response distances also occurred but were comparatively uncommon.
